Article Title: NPF gets most, BJP second as 111 MPs, MLAs switch parties since 2022: ADR
Article Text:
At least 111 sitting MPs and MLAs changed political parties after being elected between 2022 and 2026

NPF received most lawmakers, BJP second

Who were the 29 lawmakers who joined BJP?

Nagaland, West Bengal account for major share of cases

NDPP, AITC and Congress recorded most exits

Not all 111 cases were individual defections

ADR cautions that list may not be exhaustive

NEW DELHI: At least 111 sitting MPs and MLAs changed political parties after being elected between 2022 and 2026, according to an analysis by the Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) and National Election Watch (NEW). The report, released on September 24, covers elections and by-elections held during the period and includes 26 Lok Sabha MPs, seven Rajya Sabha MPs and 78 MLAs.The cases span 17 states and Union Territories, with Nagaland recording the highest number at 32, followed by West Bengal with 20, Telangana with nine, and Goa and Punjab with eight each. Maharashtra and Meghalaya recorded six cases each, Manipur five, Arunachal Pradesh and Gujarat four each, Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan two each, while Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Sikkim, Uttar Pradesh and Delhi recorded one each.Of the 111 lawmakers, 32 joined the Naga People's Front (NPF), accounting for 29 per cent of the total. The BJP received 29, or 26 per cent, followed by the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI) with 20, or 18 per cent.The Congress received nine lawmakers, or 8 per cent, while Shiv Sena received eight, or 7 per cent. NPP received six, or 5 per cent, and the People's Party of Arunachal (PPA) received four, or 4 per cent.Together, NPF, BJP and NCPI accounted for 81 of the 111 lawmakers, or 73 per cent.The NPF's figure was largely linked to the political realignment involving the Nationalist Democratic Progressive Party (NDPP) and NPF in Nagaland. ADR classifies party mergers separately from individual defections, making the distinction important when reading the overall figures.Of the 29 lawmakers listed as having joined the BJP, seven were Rajya Sabha MPs and 22 were MLAs. No Lok Sabha MP in the ADR dataset moved to the BJP.The seven Rajya Sabha MPs were originally elected from the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP): Swati Maliwal, Ashok Mittal, Harbhajan Singh, Raghav Chadha, Sandeep Kumar Pathak, Vikramjit Singh Sahney and Rajinder Gupta. The seven AAP MPs subsequently joined the BJP in April 2026.Among the MLAs were eight Congress legislators from Goa, four Congress legislators from Gujarat and two from Himachal Pradesh. The report also lists five JD(U) MLAs from Manipur as having moved to the BJP.Other BJP entrants included Samajwadi Party MLA Manoj Kumar Pandey from Uttar Pradesh, Congress MLA Nirmala Sapre from Madhya Pradesh and Karnataka MLA G Janardhan Reddy, whose Kalyana Rajya Pragathi Paksha (KRPP) merged with the BJP, according to the ADR analysis.Four Gujarat Congress MLAs, CJ Chavda, Arjun Modhwadia, Arvind Ladani and Chirag Patel, resigned, joined the BJP and subsequently contested by-elections.Nagaland recorded 32 cases, all involving MLAs. The cases were largely linked to the NDPP-NPF realignment, with 25 representatives originally elected from the NDPP among those who changed parties and 32 lawmakers joining the NPF.West Bengal recorded 20 cases, all involving Lok Sabha MPs. All 20 were originally elected on AITC tickets and subsequently moved to the NCPI, according to the analysis. The MPs have claimed a merger with the NCPI, with the matter pending before Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla.Telangana recorded nine cases, all involving MLAs originally elected from the BRS, while Congress emerged as the principal recipient. Goa recorded eight cases involving Congress MLAs who moved to the BJP. Punjab also recorded eight cases, including six Rajya Sabha members and two MLAs.Maharashtra recorded six cases, all involving Lok Sabha MPs elected from Shiv Sena (Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) who subsequently moved to Shiv Sena led by Eknath Shinde. Meghalaya recorded six MLA cases, while Manipur recorded five.Among the parties from which lawmakers moved, NDPP recorded the highest number of exits, with 25, or 23 per cent of the total. AITC followed with 20, or 18 per cent, while Congress accounted for 19, or 17 per cent.BRS recorded nine exits, or 8 per cent. AAP and NCP each accounted for seven, or 6 per cent, while Shiv Sena (Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) accounted for six, or 5 per cent. JD(U) recorded five, or 5 per cent, and NPP four, or 4 per cent.Together, NDPP, AITC and Congress accounted for 64 of the 111 lawmakers who changed parties, or 58 per cent.ADR's analysis divides the 111 cases into four categories based on how the change took place.The first covers individual switches or defections, where a legislator voluntarily leaves one party and joins another without resigning from the House.The second covers party mergers, where the original party or a substantial section of its legislative wing formally merges with another party, such as the NDPP-NPF case in Nagaland.The third covers resignation followed by a by-election, where a legislator resigns from the Assembly or Parliament, joins another party and subsequently contests and wins a by-election.The fourth covers disqualification followed by a by-election, where a member is disqualified under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution, later joins another party and wins the seat again through a by-election.ADR also noted that recent defections had been associated with the fall of governments in some State Assemblies.ADR and NEW said they made every effort to identify and include all relevant cases but cautioned that the list may not be exhaustive because of the lack of systematically maintained and readily accessible official data on lawmakers changing political parties. Other relevant cases may therefore not have been included.The previous ADR report on MPs and MLAs who changed parties was released on September 9, 2021, and covered the period from 2014 to 2021.
Article Summary: At least 111 sitting MPs and MLAs changed political parties between 2022 and 2026. Nagaland recorded the highest number at 32, followed by West Bengal with 20, Telangana with nine, and Goa and Punjab with eight each. Of the 111 lawmakers, 32 joined the Naga People's Front (NPF), accounting for 29 per cent of the total.

NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Saturday said all decisions taken on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, including the nationwide exercise, were approved unanimously, while announcing measures to simplify the process for voters facing notices over discrepancies.The clarification comes amid row over report that claimed differences within the EC over SIR of electoral rolls."In the recent months, the Commission has taken numerous decisions including SIR across the country. The order for the SIR issued on 24.6.2025 for all the States/UTs, starting with Bihar, followed by West Bengal and 30 other States/UTs was issued with the unanimous approval of the Commission. The same has been upheld by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India vide its order dated 27.5.2026. The schedule for SIR for 12 States and UTs was issued on 27.10.2025 and those for 19 States/UTs was issued on 14.05.2026 with the unanimous approval of the Commission. The final figure of number of electors will be known only after final publication in the remaining 12 states of Phase-III," the poll body said in a statement.At a meeting held on Saturday, the Commission decided that voters who receive notices during the ongoing SIR over being unmapped or having logical discrepancies will not ordinarily have to appear before the electoral registration officer (ERO).Booth-level officers (BLOs) will visit their homes to collect documents and upload them on ECINet for the ERO to decide.Hearings will be held only in exceptional cases, preferably online. An adult family member can also attend a hearing on behalf of the elector if authorised. The Commission said facilities for online hearings would be strengthened.The Commission also directed district election officers to set up help desks and special camps for people living in night shelters, labourers, poor people and homeless persons, depending on local requirements.The EC said SIR has been completed in 20 states and Union territories, including Bihar and West Bengal. It said voters whose names were left out during or after the exercise, as well as young and first-time voters, can apply to the concerned ERO for inclusion through continuous updation. Chief Electoral Officers (CEOs), DEOs and EROs have been directed to launch a special enrolment drive.The Commission also clarified that a letter sent to the Cabinet Secretary was not related to any policy decision concerning the Commission or its IT division, but concerned the functioning of an officer on deputation to the EC.It said work redistribution orders issued by the officer were not implemented after directions from two Commissioners, and oversight of the IT division by the Deputy Election Commissioner was never withdrawn.The EC said field officers have role-based access to the ECINet system based on their statutory powers. A committee headed by a senior Deputy Election Commissioner and including an independent IIT/IIIT expert will review the system for compliance with relevant laws and rules.The Commission also said future initiatives involving IT modules and portals would be discussed by the Committee of Officers before being placed for approval.The Commission extended the deadline for filing claims and objections in Delhi till October 30, following a request from the Delhi CEO. The deadline for disposal of notices and claims and objections has been extended till November 30.In Maharashtra, the deadline for filing claims and objections has been extended till October 12, while their disposal will continue till November 10.The Commission further said the SIR order issued on June 24, 2025, covering all states and UTs and subsequently implemented in phases, had received unanimous approval. It added that the Supreme Court upheld the order on May 27, 2026.In Goa, the EC said BLOs had been directed to visit voters left out of the rolls and collect their forms. Of 97 such voters, 81 have already filled Form 6 for inclusion.The Commission also directed that agendas for its meetings be circulated in advance and minutes issued, while requiring officers' annual performance reports to be completed by December 31 each year. It further said Commission approval would be required for official foreign trips and that directions issued by Commissioners to officers must be complied with.
Article Summary: The Election Commission on Saturday said all decisions taken on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, including the nationwide exercise, were approved unanimously. The Commission also announced measures to simplify the process for voters facing notices over discrepancies. The clarification comes amid row over report that claimed differences within the EC.

NEW DELHI: Union home and cooperation minister Amit Shah on Sunday flagged off India’s first LNG-powered train in Gujarat and launched a series of railway projects worth more than Rs 1,542 crore at Sabarmati The LNG-based train uses a diesel-LNG dual-fuel system, with two 1,400 HP Driving Power Cars at the Sabarmati Integrated Coaching Depot converted to run on both fuels. LNG can replace nearly 40 per cent of diesel consumption under the system.The initiative is aimed at reducing diesel use and fuel costs while lowering emissions including carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulate matter.The train was among several railway projects launched by Shah in Sabarmati, with the package also focusing on railway safety, line capacity and freight operations.Shah also laid the foundation stone for the indigenous Kavach automatic train protection system across 404 km of railway network in the Ahmedabad division.The project, estimated to cost around Rs 411 crore, covers 157 km of the Ahmedabad-Palanpur section and 247 km of the Ahmedabad-Samakhiyali section. Kavach is designed to help prevent train collisions, protect against overspeeding and reduce risks linked to human error.An automatic block signalling system has also been introduced across 122.57 km of railway sections between Sabarmati-Kalol-Bhandu Motidau and Sabarmati-Sanand-Jakhwada at a cost of around Rs 118.83 crore. The system is designed to maintain safe distances between trains and increase route capacity.Shah also inaugurated the WAG-12 locomotive maintenance shed at Sabarmati, built at an estimated cost of Rs 700 crore.The facility will provide maintenance for 300 high-horsepower WAG-12 electric locomotives, which have a capacity of around 12,000 HP and are designed to haul heavy and long freight trains.The Sabarmati-Sarkhej railway line doubling project, estimated at Rs 313.27 crore, will cover a 21-km stretch and is targeted for completion by March 2028.The project covers stations including Sabarmati, Gandhigram, Vastrapur and Sarkhej and includes bridges and road underpasses.The doubling is expected to improve train movement and connectivity towards the Sarkhej-Dholera region while supporting industrial and commercial activity in the area.The projects launched in Gujarat are aimed at improving railway safety, increasing operational capacity and promoting alternative-fuel technology in rail transport.
Article Summary: Union home and cooperation minister Amit Shah on Sunday flagged off India’s first LNG-powered train in Gujarat. Shah also launched a series of railway projects worth more than Rs 1,542 crore at Sabarmati. LNG can replace nearly 40 per cent of diesel consumption under the system.

NEET-PG 2026 result out

NEW DELHI: National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) Thursday declared NEET-PG 2026 result, with 2,65,960 candidates having appeared in the exam held in two phases this year. The result includes candidates' raw scores and overall NEET-PG ranks, reports Anuja Jaiswal.The qualifying percentile criteria remain unchanged from last year. For General and EWS categories, qualifying level was 50th percentile, with cut-off score at 262 marks out of 720 this year. It was 45th percentile and 244 marks for General Persons with Benchmark Disabilities (PwBD), and 40th percentile and 226 marks for SC, ST and OBC candidates, including PwBD candidates from these categories.In 2025, the corresponding qualifying criteria were also 50th, 45th and 40th percentiles, with cut-off scores of 276, 255 and 235, respectively, when the exam was scored out of 800. NEET-PG was conducted on Aug 30 for admission to MD, MS, DNB, DrNB Direct 6-year courses and PG Medical Diploma courses for 2026-27.NBEMS said NEET-PG rank represents overall merit position of a candidate among those who appeared for the exam and is based on actual marks scored and applicable tie-breaking criteria. The board also said each question in both papers was reviewed by faculty members from the specialty areas and none was found to be technically incorrect. Scorecards can be downloaded from NBEMS website on or after Oct 1. The answer key will be published on or after Oct 1.

Qualifying percentile criteria remain unchanged from last year. NEET was conducted on Aug 30 for admission to MD, MS, DNB, DrNB Direct 6-year courses.

NEW DELHI: Elections are, by their very nature, a contest.Political parties fight for ground, candidates wage fierce campaigns and voters ultimately decide whom to trust with their mandate.Through it all, the Election Commission is meant to stand apart and monitor the process. Its role is to frame the rules, enforce them fairly and ensure that the contest remains even-handed.Yet, in recent days, the spotlight has moved away from those fighting the election and towards the institution meant to referee it.The players are no longer the only ones under scrutiny. Increasingly, the referee itself has become the subject of the debate.A report in The Indian Express claimed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi repeatedly raised objections with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over decisions and communications that they said were issued without their knowledge or approval.The Election Commission has rejected the suggestion that the episode points to a breakdown in its functioning. It has maintained that differences of opinion are a normal part of institutional deliberation and that all final decisions of the Commission have been unanimous.That leaves a larger constitutional question at the heart of the controversy: how is India's election watchdog actually supposed to function?Is the Chief Election Commissioner the boss of the Election Commission, or simply the first among three equals? What happens when the three commissioners disagree? And why has the law governing their appointment become a subject of such intense controversy?On September 23, The Indian Express reported that Sandhu and Joshi had, on multiple occasions, objected to decisions and communications they said were taken or issued without their prior knowledge.According to the report, the two commissioners recorded such objections on at least 14 occasions over the past 10 months.The issues reportedly ranged from changes to electoral forms and access to the voter database to the allocation of work within the Commission and the filing of appeals involving electoral rolls.The report has since triggered a wider debate over whether the Election Commission's three members are exercising their powers collectively, as the law envisages, or whether the CEC has acquired a greater role in practice.According to the Indian Express report, the concerns raised by Sandhu and Joshi covered several aspects of the Commission's functioning.Taken together, the reported objections raise a question that goes beyond any individual decision: how does a three-member constitutional body exercise collective authority when its members do not initially agree?The Election Commission strongly rejected the suggestion that its internal differences amount to a breakdown in decision-making, and added that all official orders and administrative directions had been issued unanimously."Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken. Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system," the ECI said in a statement."In recent months, the Commission has taken numerous decisions, issued instructions, introduced around 40 new initiatives and undertaken many electoral reforms, including the conduct of electoral roll revision (including SIR) across the country. All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full Commission in the past one year," the poll body added.It also criticised the media report, saying that highlighting specific internal notes over a period of 10 months gives only one part of the picture."Highlighting certain specific internal notes/observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives give only one part of the picture," it said.The disagreement, therefore, is not simply over whether commissioners have expressed reservations. It is over what those reservations mean for the functioning of the institution as a whole.This is where the 2023 law becomes important.Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, provides that the Commission may, by unanimous decision, regulate how its business is conducted and allocate work among the CEC and the other Election Commissioners.It also says that, as far as possible, the Commission's business should be transacted unanimously.But it makes an important provision for situations in which consensus is not possible.If the CEC and the other Election Commissioners differ on a matter, the issue is to be decided according to the opinion of the majority.In other words, the statutory framework does not make the CEC an executive superior to the other two commissioners. The three constitute the Commission collectively, while the CEC is the "first among equals".The CEC can have a distinct role within the institution, but the law does not provide for a system in which the CEC's view automatically prevails over the other two commissioners.Where the three disagree, the majority view is the deciding view.The controversy now centres on whether some of the decisions cited in the recent report were, in practice, implemented despite objections from the other two commissioners, and if so, how that squares with the statutory scheme governing the Commission's decision-making.The current controversy also brings back an older and deeper question: Who should appoint the people who conduct India's elections?In March 2023, the Supreme Court ruled that Parliament had not yet enacted a law governing appointments to the Election Commission, despite Article 324 of the Constitution envisaging such a framework.Until Parliament enacted such a law, a Constitution bench prescribed an interim selection mechanism comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha and the Chief Justice of India.The court stressed that an independent Election Commission was essential for democracy and observed that those entrusted with conducting elections must be insulated from executive influence.Parliament subsequently enacted the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.But the new law changed the composition of the selection committee.Instead of the Chief Justice of India, it provided for a Union Cabinet minister nominated by the Prime Minister. The committee therefore consists of the Prime Minister, a Union minister nominated by him and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha.The opposition has alleged that the 2023 Act gives the executive “overwhelming” control over the appointment of Election Commissioners. The government, meanwhile, has defended the law and its institutional framework.The dispute has now reached the Supreme Court, where a challenge to the validity of the appointment law produced a split verdict.A two-judge SC bench differed over whether the matter should immediately be referred to a Constitution bench. Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma disagreed on that question, although both agreed that the matter should ultimately be placed before the Chief Justice of India for consideration by a larger bench.They also agreed that sending the case first to a three-judge bench would be of "little worth" and could further delay a final determination of the constitutional questions involved. The matter is likely to be heard by a 5-judge bench soon.The issue is vital as it extends beyond the current dispute inside the Election Commission. It touches a larger institutional question: How independent should the body conducting India's elections be from the executive, and what safeguards should govern the appointment of those who head it?The latest controversy has also acquired a political dimension, with opposition parties preparing fresh notices seeking the removal of CEC Gyanesh Kumar.According to media reports, the notices, being drafted and vetted by experts, are expected to be submitted in the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha next week. The proposed notices are expected to include issues raised in the Indian Express report.This would not be the opposition's first attempt.On April 7, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairperson CP Radhakrishnan rejected an earlier notice seeking Kumar's removal. That notice had been signed by 130 Lok Sabha members and 63 Rajya Sabha members and alleged partisanship and arbitrariness in the conduct of the SIR exercise.Separately, a notice submitted by 73 opposition MPs in the Rajya Sabha on April 24 seeking Kumar's removal remains pending in the Upper House.But removing a CEC is deliberately difficult.Article 324(5) of the Constitution provides that the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only "in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court".The same protection is incorporated into Section 11(2) of the 2023 Act.The other Election Commissioners enjoy a different safeguard: they cannot be removed from office except on the recommendation of the CEC.The higher threshold for removing a CEC is intended to protect the office from arbitrary or politically motivated removal.The removal process is rooted in the constitutional procedure applicable to Supreme Court judges.Article 124(4) of the Constitution, which lays down the procedure for removing a Supreme Court judge, states that a judge can be removed only by an order of the President following an address by each House of Parliament.Such an address must be supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of at least two-thirds of members present and voting, in the same session, on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.The process begins with a notice of motion in either House of Parliament alleging misbehaviour or incapacity. The notice must be signed by at least 100 MPs in the Lok Sabha or 50 MPs in the Rajya Sabha.The presiding officer of the concerned House can admit or refuse the motion after considering the material and information available. If the motion is admitted, an inquiry is conducted into the charges by a committee constituted for the purpose.If the charges are established, the motion must be passed by a majority of the total membership of each House and by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting in both Houses.Once both Houses pass the motion in accordance with these requirements, an address is made to the President, who then issues the order removing the CEC.The President's role at this stage is constitutional and formal once Parliament has passed the required address.The current structure of the Election Commission is itself the product of an institutional evolution.When the ECI was established in 1950, it was a single-member body, with the Chief Election Commissioner as its sole member.It became a three-member body for the first time in 1989, but that arrangement was short-lived. In January 1990, the VP Singh government reverted the Commission to a single-member structure.The system changed again in October 1993, when the PV Narasimha Rao government appointed MS Gill and GVG Krishnamurthy as Election Commissioners alongside CEC TN Seshan.Seshan challenged the appointments in the Supreme Court, arguing that the addition of commissioners diluted the authority of the CEC.In its 1995 judgment, a Constitution bench upheld the multi-member structure.The court made clear that the CEC was not institutionally superior to the other Election Commissioners. The three were intended to function collectively, with differences being resolved through the decision-making mechanism of the Commission.That judgment established the broad institutional framework that exists today.The Election Commission is not designed as a hierarchy in which one person commands and two others merely assist. Nor is it simply three independent offices operating in parallel. It is a constitutional body meant to function collectively.The law provides for unanimity where possible and a majority where consensus fails.The CEC occupies the position of first among equals, rather than that of a superior authority.The significance of the current controversy, therefore, lies not merely in the existence of disagreements within the Commission. Differences are inevitable in any institution exercising such enormous constitutional responsibility.The larger question is what happens after those differences arise: whether they remain part of an internal deliberative process, as the ECI maintains, or whether they reflect a deeper dispute over how collective authority is being exercised.The credibility of an election does not rest only on the final tally of votes.It also rests on whether voters believe that the rules were applied fairly, the institutions enforcing them remained above the contest and the process was conducted without favour or hidden influence.The Election Commission, therefore, carries a burden that goes beyond administering polls: it must command confidence across the political spectrum and among voters themselves. Any perception that the referee is divided, opaque or partisan can cast a shadow over the process, even when the electoral machinery continues to function formally within the law.In the end, public trust is not built merely by declaring an election free and fair; it is built by ensuring that voters have little reason to doubt that verdict.

They also raised concerns about whether statutory authorities responsible for maintaining electoral rolls had complete access to voter data on the ERONet portal. Article Text:

NEW DELHI: With EPFO increasing the mandatory wage ceiling from Rs 15,000 a month to Rs 25,000, employees will now contribute Rs 3,000 (at 12% contribution of Rs 25,000 wage) towards their PF savings from Rs 1,800 earlier, govt said in a set of FAQs released. This will be along with a contribution of Rs 917 by employers (at 3.67%), up from Rs 550, taking the mandatory monthly PF contributions to Rs 3,917.In addition, Rs 2,083 - an 8.3% contribution from employers' share - will now go towards the pension kitty from earlier Rs 1,250. On Sept 17, govt increased EPFO wage ceiling to bring one crore additional workers into the social security net as minimum wages in at least seven states and UTs - Delhi, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Haryana, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Uttarakhand - have crossed the Rs 15,000 threshold.In the case of an employee with a monthly wage of Rs 20,000, the mandatory PF contribution will be Rs 3,134 - the employee share Rs 2,400 and the employer share Rs 734, with an additional Rs 1,666 going towards EPS from employer's share. But if an employee earns, say, Rs 35,000 a month, the mandatory PF contribution will be Rs 6,000 (Rs 3,000 from employee and employers each), with no amount going towards pension as EPS is available only to those whose wages do not exceed the EPFO wage ceiling.The retirement savings agency said the new regime kicked in from Sept 17 and asked employers to review contractor compliance, wherever contract labour is engaged, and update its payroll systems.Allaying employee fears of attempts to pass on the contribution by deducting more from salaries, it said an employer's statutory contribution cannot simply be treated as an employee deduction merely by describing it as part of CTC.While the move will likely increase compliance costs for small and medium enterprises, the potential costs due to the rise in the wage ceiling can be partly offset by the incentive of up to Rs 3,000 per month for every additional employment created under PM Viksit Bharat Rojgar Yojana.
Article Summary: EPFO increasing mandatory wage ceiling from Rs 15,000 a month to Rs 25,000. Employees will now contribute Rs 3,000 towards their PF savings from Rs 1,800 earlier. This will be along with a contribution of Rs 917 by employers (at 3.67%), up from Rs 550.

NEW DELHI: India has called for a global system that ensures countries sharing pathogens and biological resources during a health emergency also get timely access to vaccines, diagnostics, medicines and technologies developed from them.The demand was made at the UN High-Level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response in New York, where India stressed that the credibility of the WHO Pandemic Agreement would depend on a fair Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing (PABS) system.Union health secretary Punya Salila Srivastava said countries contributing pathogens should receive the benefits arising from their use, while respecting national sovereignty. She also said ongoing negotiations on the PABS system should not be prejudged and that implementation should take into account national circumstances and capacities.Drawing on its experience during Covid-19, India also called for digital public infrastructure to be recognised as a global public good, citing its role in disease surveillance, vaccination, risk communication, supply chains and continuity of health services during the pandemic.India highlighted its contribution during Covid, saying it supplied 300 million vaccine doses to around 100 countries and two UN entities, besides providing medical assistance to more than 150 countries.At the meeting, India also outlined measures to strengthen pandemic preparedness, including expanding laboratory networks, emergency coordination, the health workforce, stockpiles and clinical care capacity.The WHO Pandemic Agreement, adopted in May 2025, is aimed at strengthening global preparedness for future pandemics. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for urgent completion of negotiations on the PABS system, saying delays could affect the world's ability to respond to future pandemics.India stressed that pandemic preparedness must remain rooted in national health systems and domestic financing, with international assistance complementing national efforts. It also called for equity and global solidarity to remain central to preparations for future outbreaks.

NEW DELHI: Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann will hold a meeting of the seven-member coordination committee constituted to examine the amended anti-sacrilege law, at his residence here on Sunday.At the meeting to be held at 1 pm, the committee will deliberate on provisions of the Jaagat Jot Sri Guru Granth Sahib Satkar (Amendment) Act, 2026 and matters related to its implementation, with an aim to uphold the highest standards of 'satkar' (reverence) for the Sikh Holy Book Guru Granth Sahib, according to an official statement issued on Saturday.All members of the coordination committee will attend the meeting.The seven-member panel comprises former Akal Takht Jathedar Giani Raghbir Singh, Sant Giani Harnaam Singh Khalsa, Sant Baba Sewa Singh, former Justices Jaswinder Singh and Gurbir Singh, former IPS officer Jatinder Singh Aulakh and Advocate Preet Inder Paul Singh.The amendment bill was unanimously passed by the Punjab Assembly on April 13. NEW DELHI: The Federation of Indian Pilots (FIP) has urged the civil aviation ministry to ensure that its technical submissions on the Air India AI171 crash are formally considered before the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) finalises its probe report.The AAIB investigation into the June 12, 2025 crash in Ahmedabad, which killed 260 people, is at an advanced stage.In a letter to civil aviation minister K Rammohan Naidu on Friday, FIP sought to be nominated as an “independent technical participant in the review of the draft AI171 final investigation report”.FIP said it had “reliably learnt that the government/ ministry has directed or is considering requiring the draft report to undergo examination by an independent committee before it is circulated/ finalised”. It said that if such a review mechanism is being constituted, the pilots' body should be formally nominated and represented as an independent technical stakeholder representing the professional pilot community.The federation also requested that its technical submissions receive formal and documented consideration before the final report is issued.The FIP had last week urged the AAIB to conduct a comprehensive evaluation of electrical-system evidence related to Boeing 787 aircraft as part of the AI171 investigation.The Air India Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner, registered as VT-ANB, crashed shortly after taking off from Ahmedabad for London Gatwick on June 12, 2025. Of the 242 people on board, 241 died, while 19 people on the ground were also killed. All 12 crew members died and one passenger survived.The aircraft, manufactured in 2013 and powered by GE engines, had flown 41,868 hours. Its Airworthiness Review Certificate was valid until May 23, 2026.In its latest update on the investigation, the AAIB said significant progress had been made and that the final report would be released after completion of all investigative activities and the required international review and consultation processes.The bureau has said the investigation team has examined technical, operational, organisational and human factors associated with the accident, without disclosing specific findings from the probe.

Article Title: 'Avoids issue of Gen Z voters': Congress attacks EC's 'wishy-washy' press note, seeks pause in SIR
Article Text:

First, the Press note does not directly deny the story or its findings. It makes a defensive attempt to downplay the same in paragraph 3(i) and 3(ii) but does not say that the allegations are baseless.

Second, in the case of Goa, after having been caught out the ECI has sheepishly stated that Form 6 has already been filled out for inclusion by 81 of the 97 deleted voters. Third, it seeks to justify the Commissions actions by appealing to the Order of the Supreme Court dated May 27th, 2026. The Order which was pronounced well before the recent revelations will not save the CEC for the malicious deletion of targeted voters, for the incompetence that has resulted in citizens being wiped off the roles, for the crores lost in both expenses and man-hours due to the confusion and harassment caused to entire families.

Fifth, the Press Release also states the ECI will now involve experts from IIT/IIIT to review the ECINET portal and submit a report to ensure it complies with rules. Aside from being a meaningless safeguard (since the concern is not about the technical soundness but rather the centralization which prevents voter addition at ground level) this confirms the concerns attributed to the two other Election Commissioners per the reportage.

Sixth, the Press Note avoids answering the questions regarding the deliberate targeting of Gen Z voters. The ECI has no answer for its targeted disenfranchisement, beginning mid-July 2026 through wholly illegal changes made to Form 6 (unseen and unapproved by Parliament) which placed an unfair burden on them to find and disclose their parents and/or grandparents’ details.

NEW DELHI: On a day when Election Commission found itself under the scanner, a two-judge bench of Supreme Court gave a split verdict on whether the issue of validity of the law on appointment of CEC/ECs be referred to a constitution bench, but later agreed to refer the case to a larger bench for the sake of early adjudication of the contentious issue.Validity of several provisions of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 has been challenged on the ground that the law gives the executive "overwhelming" power to appoint its nominee as election commissioner, as the selection panel composed of the PM, a Cabinet minister and the leader of the opposition is designed to give govt a 2:1 majority. The petitioners contended that EC's independence would be compromised in this process.The 2023 law was framed to replace an SC verdict which had directed that selection be done by a committee of the PM, CJI and leader of the opposition until Parliament determined the composition by passing a law. "Speaking in one voice would have better served institutional cohesion. Unfortunately, the court is divided in its opinion," a bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and S C Sharma said.The hearing in the case went on for five days and at the fag end of proceedings, the Centre had sought referral of the case to a constitution bench.Noting that appointment of CEC/ECs was being litigated for last 11 years in SC after a petition was filed in 2015, the bench decided that the case should not be referred to a three-judge bench, which is the normal procedure, but to a constitution bench to settle the issue once and for all. It reasoned that a decision by a three-judge bench would be of little worth and only delay adjudication of the significant issue(s) that these writ petitions raise."Thus, we direct that the papers be placed before the CJI for considering the desirability of constituting a constitution bench of such number of judges to decide the question of vires of Sec 7 and the other provisions of Act," the bench said.The bench expressed hope that the case would be given priority as the issues raised were of "foundational importance to the democratic fabric of the country and its citizenry"."Petitioners seem to be justified in expressing their anxiety that references to five-judge benches remain unresolved for years. If statistics are any guide, none can say with any reasonable degree of certainty when long-pending references will get resolved. Undisputedly, this is an area of grave concern and the inordinate delay in resolution of the references is itself a source of institutional embarrassment which all stakeholders ought to strive to avoid. Self-introspection, indeed, is required," it said."We, thus, take this opportunity of requesting the Chief Justice to also explore the necessity of constituting a permanent five-judge bench to decide pure constitutional issues. This is not something novel that we are saying. It has been opined time and again by responsible citizens and we simply endorse their opinion. Given that resolving constitutional issues is the primary task of judges of this court, that must remain its core priority.Pendency of references for far too long, any period between five and 20 years or more, does not reflect well on the institution. It is time that the institution addresses the issue with the urgency and promptitude it deserves," the bench said.
Article Summary: Two-judge bench of Supreme Court gave a split verdict on whether the issue of validity of the law on appointment of CEC/ECs be referred to a constitution bench. The bench later agreed to refer the case to a larger bench for the sake of early adjudication of the contentious issue.

Article Title: In 2024, 75-year-old Iowa farmer Evie Haupt said three wind turbines on her 160 acres were bringing in about $35,000 a year while using under 3 acres and had helped reduce $350,000 in farm debt to $67
Article Text:
A financial lifeline for rural landowners

The explosive expansion of Iowa wind power

Addressing local pushback and debate

On a 160-acre farm in central Iowa, three tall wind turbines quietly rise above the fields. Each turbine uses less than an acre of land, but together they provide an annual income that has changed the financial future of 75-year-old farmer Evie Haupt. According to a CBS News report by Janet Shamlian and Alicia Hastey, Haupt earns about $35,000 each year by leasing part of her land for the wind turbines. The income rises with inflation and has helped her pay down a $350,000 farm debt left after her husband died a decade ago. Her remaining debt is now $67,000. For many family farms across the United States, extra sources of income have become important lifelines. The U.S. Department of Agriculture expects farm profits to fall by 25 per cent, as farmers face higher costs, changing crop prices and unpredictable weather. Adding wind power to traditional farming can provide steady income and help protect farmers from financial shocks.Farm debt can force families to make difficult choices, including selling land that has been passed down through generations. Haupt faced a major financial challenge after her husband died, leaving behind hundreds of thousands of dollars in farm debt.Payments from the wind turbines gave her a steady source of money that could go toward those loans. Each turbine uses less than an acre, so Haupt can still farm most of her 160 acres. This gives her two sources of income from the same land, while using only a small part of the property for the turbines. The payments can also rise over time because the contracts include inflation adjustments. This helps protect landowners as prices and other costs change. For Haupt, the result has been major. She has paid off more than 80 per cent of her farm debt while keeping the land in use.Iowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Iowa had only a few hundred wind turbines 20 years ago. Today, it has more than 6,000, producing about 60 per cent of the state's energy. Across the United States, more than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Federal energy officials also say current U.S. wind power cuts carbon emissions by an amount equal to taking 73 million passenger vehicles off the road. Attorney Kathy Law, who grew up on a farm and married a farmer, has helped place nearly half of Iowa's wind turbines. Her work in energy law grew from her own family's experience with farming. Law wanted to study law while she was in high school, but the severe farm crisis of the 1980s kept her home to help with the family farm. She later went to law school in her forties. She graduated on the same day her son finished high school and later served as president of the Iowa Wind Energy Association for three years. "From my farm background, I think I can talk their talk and have conversations with landowners that are interested in having wind turbines on their property," Law told CBS News.The rapid growth of wind power in rural communities has also brought opposition in some counties. Local critics say wind turbines can change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats. Law believes landowners should be able to decide what happens on their property. "Nobody's requiring them to put that on their farms or on their land," Law said during her interview with CBS News. "We want to be able to put turbines on our land and receive those benefits. " Haupt has a similar view of the changes to her farm. While she remains attached to traditional farming, she sees clean energy as an important step for rural communities. "I look at it as progress," Haupt told CBS News. "I think we can't stand in the way of progress." For Haupt, giving up a very small part of her land to produce electricity makes sense for her finances and for the wider community. "I need to give up one or two acres of my land so that I can generate a commodity that we all use every day, and we all want to use more of it every day," Haupt said. "So I'm happy to be able to be a part of that generation."
Article Summary: Iowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. More than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating in the U.S. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Critics say wind turbines change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats.

Article Title: India loses 6.2 million LPG customers in months, connections drop from 333.9 million to 327.7 million, reversing a decade of growth as Iran war squeezes Gulf supplies and oil firms halt new connection
Article Text:
Oil ministry data showed that active domestic LPG customers stood at 327.7 million at the beginning of September.

LPG connections drop

PNG push

The US-Iran war has hit LPG imports and as a result India's domestic LPG customer base has declined for the first time in more than a decade. Around 6.2 million households have dropped off between April and August. The contraction came as the Iran war disrupted supplies, prompting oil companies to stop issuing new connections and tighten checks on existing customers.The decline has taken place against the backdrop of the Iran war and its impact on LPG availability from the Gulf region. Before the war, the region accounted for around 90% of India's LPG imports.Oil ministry data showed that active domestic LPG customers stood at 327.7 million at the beginning of September, down from 333.9 million at the start of April. The number of beneficiaries under the government's Ujjwala scheme for poor households also declined, falling by around 0.6 million to 105.7 million, according to an ET report.The fall marks a reversal after years of steady expansion in LPG adoption. At the start of 2015-16, India had 148.6 million active LPG customers. That number had more than doubled to 333.9 million by the beginning of the current fiscal year.LPG customer growth was particularly strong in the four years through 2018-19, when it ranged between 11.9% and 19.6%.As the customer base became larger, however, the pace moderated to around 5% or lower. In the current fiscal year, instead of growing, the customer base has contracted by 1%.With supplies becoming tighter, oil marketing companies stopped issuing new connections to households and began using Aadhaar-based biometric verification to identify inactive customers, multiple LPG connections within the same family and households that already had access to piped natural gas (PNG), industry executives said.At the same time, the government has been encouraging households in areas where PNG infrastructure is available to move from LPG to natural gas.City gas distribution companies added nearly 0.6 million PNG customers during the current fiscal year through July, taking the overall number to 17.5 million. Billed customers provide a different measure of the shift, with their number rising by 1.06 million to 10.7 million.The move to PNG accounts for roughly one-sixth of the 6.2 million decline in LPG customers.The largest regional fall came in southern India, where the LPG customer base declined by 2.63 million from the end of March. Western India followed with a reduction of 1.62 million, while northern India saw its customer base fall by 1.5 million.Eastern India recorded a decline of 0.34 million customers.Despite the contraction, northern India remained the region with the largest LPG customer base at the beginning of September, with 99.3 million customers. Southern India had 79.8 million, western India 68.3 million and eastern India 67.5 million.India's LPG use has risen sharply over the past few years. Consumption stood at 31.3 million tonnes in FY25, up from 29.7 million tonnes a year earlier. Domestic output, however, has not kept pace and has remained broadly unchanged at around 12.8 million tonnes.Initial estimates for FY26 point to LPG consumption of about 28 million tonnes, while domestic production is expected to be around 10.7 million tonnes. The numbers again leave a substantial shortfall that has to be met through imports.The widening gap between what India consumes and what it produces domestically has increased the country's dependence on imports to meet LPG requirements, making the fuel one of the more import-reliant components of its energy basket.The supply disruption has also brought another limitation into focus: India's relatively small LPG storage capacity.Storing LPG is more complicated and costly than storing crude oil because the fuel has to be maintained in liquid form under pressure. This means storage requires specialised facilities, including pressurised cylinders, spherical tanks and underground caverns.India is estimated to have a total LPG storage capacity of around 1.9 million tonnes, which is equivalent to roughly 22 days of supply.The expansion of storage infrastructure has been constrained by the high cost of building such facilities, geological limitations and the geographically dispersed nature of LPG distribution. With demand rising rapidly, storage capacity has not expanded at the same pace.
Article Summary: India's domestic LPG customer base has declined for the first time in more than a decade. Around 6.2 million households have dropped off between April and August. The contraction came as the Iran war disrupted supplies, prompting oil companies to stop issuing new connections.

Article Title: He attested brother’s sale deed decades ago; Madras HC cites it as evidence of oral partition, rejects family’s claim to 3.5 acres of ancestral land
Article Text:
The dispute arose when his grandchildren challenged the nature of the original purchase. (Image for representative purpose only)

What the case is about

Why did the family lose the case?

What is the validity of oral partition in property related cases, especially when related documents support the claim? A recent judgment of the Madras High Court is important in this regard since it lays down a key principle: when a person formally attests or signs a sale deed involving a family member, in this case, a brother, it is presumed that the person was aware of the contents of the document and understood the transaction. Such a person cannot later claim that they had no knowledge of the details of the deal.The ruling had significant consequences for the children of a family. They ultimately lost their claim over 3.5 acres of ancestral land and were left with only 50 cents.The dispute goes back to a family who had four sons. In 1944, the eldest son purchased 4 acres and 1 cent of land through a sale deed in Tamil Nadu. During the proceedings before the Madras High Court, it was established that he had acquired the property in his capacity as the eldest son and manager of the joint family. The purchase was made using income generated from the joint family and its properties and was for the benefit of the family.The court also found in 1950, that the eldest brother orally partitioned the property among himself and his three brothers. Each of his three brothers received 1 acre, accounting for 3 acres in total, while he retained 1 acre.Subsequently, in 1963, he sold 51 cents from the portion that he had retained to a third party.As a result, the property remaining with his family was reduced to around 50 cents. This was after accounting for the original 4 acres and 1 cent, the 3 acres distributed among his three brothers and the 51 cents that he later sold.The dispute arose when his grandchildren challenged the nature of the original purchase, according to an ET report. They claimed that he had acquired the entire 4 acres and 1 cent using his own money, making it his self-acquired property rather than joint ancestral property, as claimed by the other side.Based on this argument, the grandchildren also disputed the validity of the oral partition between their grandfathers. Their contention was that if the partition itself was invalid, the subsequent transfers of the 3 acres, with 1 acre going to each brother, would also have no legal validity.There was another important development in the history of the property. The entire 3 acres allotted to the three brothers eventually came into the possession of a temple through sale deeds and/or gift deeds executed by the respective brothers.The land sold by the eldest brother to a third party in 1963 followed a similar course. The person who purchased the 51 cents later transferred that land to the temple as well.Consequently, the temple ended up with 3 acres and 50 cents of the original property, while the family of the elder son was left with 50 cents.The grandchildren challenged the temple’s claim over the land that had ultimately come into its possession through the various transfers.On September 11, 2026, the Madras High Court ruled in favour of the temple. The temple consequently retained the 3 acres and 50 cents of land, while the grandchildren retained the remaining 50 cents, the ET report said.A key factor that went against the grandchildren was the eldest brother’s own signature on the sale deed executed by his brother. As noted earlier, each of the three brothers had received 1 acre under the 1950 oral partition. One of them subsequently sold his 1-acre share through a sale deed in 1961. Significantly, the eldest brother himself signed and attested that document.The Madras High Court took particular note of the fact that while the other brothers had used their thumb impressions, the eldest brother had signed the document. This indicated to the court that he was the most educated among the brothers and consequently lent greater significance to his signature on the sale deed.The court held that he would have read and understood the contents of the sale deed before signing it. Since he did not raise any objection to the transaction, the court concluded that he was aware of and accepted the 1950 oral partition. This, in turn, supported the finding that the property was joint family ancestral property rather than his self-acquired property.The Madras High Court held that the temple had established its case and that the disputed property was joint family property. According to the court, the land had been purchased in the name of the eldest brother in his capacity as the kartha of the joint family. The court also found, on the basis of the preponderance of probabilities, that the oral partition had taken place. In contrast, the defendants, failed to establish their case satisfactorily.The court, therefore, held that the sale deeds executed by his brothers, or their legal representatives, in respect of the portions allotted to them under the oral partition, described as Suit 'C' and 'D' properties, were valid and binding on him.Sameena Chatrapathy, Partner, DSK Legal, told ET that the central issue in the dispute was whether the oral partition and the transfers that followed it were legally valid and binding.In this case, although the property had been purchased in an individual’s name on paper, it was nevertheless treated as joint family property and therefore became subject to a subsequent oral partition.The same portion of the property was effectively transferred on two occasions on different legal premises. It was first dealt with as self-acquired property and was subsequently dealt with as joint family property, on the basis that it had been purchased using family funds and that title had passed through the oral partition. The two transactions involved different recipients.Chatrapathy explained that whether an oral partition is valid depends on the facts and circumstances surrounding the arrangement. In this Madras High Court matter, the eldest brother had signed as a witness to the sale by his brother.His signature appeared on the conveyance relating to the portion of land that his brother had obtained through the oral partition. This supported the conclusion that the property was joint family property, that the oral partition was valid and, consequently, that the transfer arising from that partition was also valid and binding.The case also carries lessons for families dealing with ancestral property. Anyone who signs as a witness to a relative’s sale deed, particularly where the document records the division of ancestral property, should not treat the signature as a mere formality when they themselves have an interest in the property.The law may regard that signature as evidence that the person knew about and accepted the contents of the document, potentially creating consequences that continue for the rest of their life.
Article Summary: The ruling had significant consequences for the children of a family. They ultimately lost their claim over 3.5 acres of ancestral land and were left with only 50 cents. A key factor that went against the grandchildren was the eldest brother’s own signature on the sale deed executed by his brother.

Article Title: Delhi SIR: Special camps on Sunday to enrol eligible voters
Article Text:
Delhi election officials will conduct special camps across polling stations on Sunday for eligible voters' inclusion





NEW DELHI: Delhi election officials will hold special camps at all polling stations across 70 assembly constituencies Sunday to help eligible voters left out of the draft SIR roll apply for inclusion. Separate camps will be organised at colleges, universities and other educational institutions on Sept 29 and 30 to enrol gen-Z voters.The camps are part of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Delhi. The office of the chief electoral officer said the Sept27 exercise would be the second special camp for left-out eligible citizens, following the first one held on Sept 20.At Sunday’s polling station camps, eligible citizens whose names are missing from the draft electoral roll can approach booth-level officers (BLOs) for assistance in submitting form 6 for inclusion.The Sept 29-30 camps at educational institutions will focus on enrolling electors aged 18 to 25 years. BLOs will be present with electoral rolls and blank form 6 forms to guide eligible students through the application process.Those who have completed or will complete 18 years of age by Oct 1, 2026, and whose names are not in the draft electoral roll can apply for inclusion along with the required supporting documents.For new electors, form 6 requires proof of age and ordinary residence. Accepted age-proof documents include a birth certificate, Aadhaar card, PAN card, driving licence, Class X or XII certificate and passport. Residence can be established through documents such as Aadhaar card, utility bills, bank or post office passbook, passport, land records, registered rent agreement or registered sale deed.Applicants must also submit the prescribed declaration form, which seeks details of the applicant and their linkage with the electoral roll of the last SIR, including details of specified relatives and their EPIC numbers, where available.Forms 6, 6A, 7 and 8 can also be submitted at the camps. Form 6 is for inclusion of new voters; form 6A is for inclusion of overseas electors; form 7 is for objections to the proposed inclusion or deletion of a name; and form 8 is for shifting of residence, correction of entries, replacement of EPIC or marking of PwD.BLOs will be available at the camps to assist electors with the filing process.
Article Summary: Delhi election officials will hold special camps at all polling stations across 70 assembly constituencies Sunday. Separate camps will be organised at colleges, universities and other educational institutions on Sept 29 and 30 to enrol gen-Z voters. The camps are part of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Delhi.

Article Title: Boeing finds software glitch that may disable landing guidance on some 737 MAX jets
Article Text:
Boeing said it had notified operators about the issue last month and was working on a permanent fix. (AP photo)

FAA reviewing potential safety issue

Latest issue adds to scrutiny of MAX

Boeing has found a previously undisclosed software problem on some 737 MAX aircraft that could leave pilots without automated flight guidance during a particular landing situation, Wall Street Journal reported citing company documents.The problem is linked to a cockpit software update and can arise when pilots change the aircraft's planned route after a missed approach. In such a situation, an automated navigation feature may stop working during the subsequent landing attempt.Boeing said it had notified operators about the issue last month and was working on a permanent fix."We shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases. Our engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue," Boeing said in an emailed statement to news agency Reuters.The US Federal Aviation Administration said it was aware of the problem involving a software update for flight computers installed on certain 737 MAX aircraft."The FAA will convene a Corrective Action Review Board and will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern," the agency said.The FAA, Boeing and airlines are now assessing how widely the affected software is being used and whether the problem presents a broader safety risk.Southwest Airlines and United Airlines have asked Boeing to hold back deliveries of new 737 MAX aircraft fitted with the affected software, instead requesting aircraft with an earlier software version, the Wall Street Journal reported.It remains unclear how many aircraft are currently operating with the software in question. The development comes as Boeing's 737 MAX programme continues to face close regulatory and safety scrutiny. The aircraft was grounded worldwide after two fatal crashes in 2018 and 2019, which together killed 346 people.Boeing also faced renewed scrutiny in January 2024 after a door plug blew out of an almost-new 737 MAX 9 operated by Alaska Airlines during a flight.The latest software issue does not mean that the aircraft is unsafe to fly. Regulators and the company are still examining the problem and determining whether any further action is required.
Article Summary: Boeing has found a previously undisclosed software problem on some 737 MAX aircraft. Problem is linked to a cockpit software update and can arise when pilots change the aircraft's planned route after a missed approach. In such a situation, an automated navigation feature may stop working during the subsequent landing attempt.

Article Title: Delhi SIR: Colleges, universities to host special voter enrolment camps for young voters on Sep 29-30
Article Text:
The chief electoral officer of Delhi is organizing special camps for voter registration on September 29 and 30 (Representative image)





NEW DELHI: The Office of the chief electoral officer (CEO), Delhi, has directed all district election officers to organise special camps at colleges, universities and other educational institutions across the national capital on September 29 and 30 as part of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) 2026.The camps will be held from 9am to 3pm on both days and will focus on maximising enrolment of young voters aged 18 to 25, news agency ANI reported.Eligible students will be encouraged to fill Form-6 for inclusion in the electoral rolls.In a letter dated September 25, deputy chief electoral officer (ER) Prashant Kumar Prasad directed all DEOs to make necessary arrangements for the camps and ensure adequate electoral rolls, Form-6 applications and other required materials are available.The CEO office also directed officials to deploy non-teaching BLOs at the camps and asked principals and heads of educational institutions to disseminate information about the camps in advance and motivate eligible students to enrol.Applications received from students seeking enrolment in another district or Assembly Constituency will be forwarded to the concerned EROs/AEROs, according to the directions, ANI reported.Officials have also been asked to maintain proper records of all forms received at colleges and institutions, publicise the camps through social media and ensure regular monitoring at the district and Assembly Constituency levels.The camps are being organised during the claims and objections period of the SIR 2026.The CEO Delhi website says eligible electors whose names are not included in the draft electoral roll can apply for inclusion through Form-6 during the claims and objections period, which runs until September 30.(With agency inputs)
Article Summary: Chief electoral officer of Delhi is organizing special camps for voter registration on September 29 and 30. The camps will be held from 9am to 3pm on both days and will focus on maximising enrolment of young voters aged 18 to 25.Eligible students will be encouraged to fill Form-6 for inclusion in electoral rolls.

Article Title: Satya Niketan collapse: Delhi govt forms high-powered panel to examine student accommodation, frame PG rules
Article Text:
A committee has been established by the Delhi govt to assess student accommodation safety following the collapse of a building in Satya Niketan





NEW DELHI: The Delhi government has constituted a high-powered committee to examine student accommodation and safety in the capital and recommend time-bound measures, the Delhi high court was informed on Friday during a hearing on the September 6 Satya Niketan building collapse.The committee has already decided to prepare a regulatory framework for paying guest (PG) accommodation and private student hostels in Delhi.The submission was made during the hearing of a matter concerning the building collapse in Satya Niketan, where a boys' paying-guest accommodation near Delhi University's South Campus had collapsed while repair work was underway, killing seven people, including five students, and injuring several others.A bench of Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia was informed by the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) that immediately after the September 6 incident, the matter was taken up at the highest executive level of the civic body.The MCD also informed the court that five officers across the entire supervisory chain of the corporation, including a deputy commissioner, had been suspended.Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, representing the Delhi government, MCD and Delhi Police, gave details of other steps taken by the authorities.The court also termed Delhi University's affidavit "absolutely vague". The varsity's counsel assured the court that a better response would be filed.According to the MCD's affidavit, the Delhi government constituted a magisterial inquiry into the collapse to examine issues including the validity of permissions, compliance with building bye-laws and the role of the concerned officials.The MCD said no sanctioned building plan had been approved for the property and that it had not been constructed pursuant to valid MCD permission.The civic body also said a time-bound survey and inspection of PG buildings identified across all 12 zones under its jurisdiction had been undertaken.Of 2,453 PG buildings surveyed, 2,342 were found to be visibly safe, 91 required minor repairs, 30 required major repairs and four were found to be in dangerous condition."In addition to that, eight load-bearing structures above ground-plus three storeys and 77 framed structures above ground-plus four storeys are being separately identified for close monitoring as the same may be vulnerable," it said.Cases involving any prima facie issue concerning immediate structural safety or danger to life are being prioritised for appropriate inspection and strict action in accordance with law, the MCD said in its affidavit.The Delhi government's High-Powered Committee on student accommodation and safety was constituted through a September 10 order to examine issues relating to student accommodation and safety in Delhi and recommend appropriate, time-bound measures."In its meeting held on September 15, the committee, among other decisions, resolved to prepare a regulatory framework for paying guest accommodations and private student hostels.It was decided that the Department of Training and Technical Education (DTTE) and the Department of Higher Education (DHE) shall jointly prepare a regulatory framework for PG accommodation and private student hostels," it said.The committee also decided that the framework would be developed in consultation with the stakeholder agency or department and should take into account the experience of other states and Union Territories in regulating PG accommodations.The Delhi Police, in its reply, said six accused, including the owners of the collapsed Satya Niketan building, had failed to take adequate safety precautions during construction or repair work, creating a situation that endangered human lives and ultimately caused deaths.It said the building collapsed due to excessive structural load or weakening of the existing structure, endangering human life and resulting in casualties.The MCD affidavit was filed in a pending PIL by law student Aniket Kumar Gupta, seeking urgent medical care and rehabilitation of affected students, Rs 1 crore compensation for the families of the deceased and preservation of crucial evidence relating to the collapse.The court permitted retired IPS officer Kiran Bedi to address it in the matter and asked the parties to also supply her with the documents they would place on record.The court listed the matter for further hearing on October 14 and said that if the Delhi government's High-Powered Committee meeting takes place in the meantime, its minutes should be placed on record.On September 7, the high court had ordered a high-level MCD inquiry into the building collapse and made it clear that the government could not evade responsibility.(With PTI inputs)
Article Summary: The committee has already decided to prepare a regulatory framework for paying guest (PG) accommodation and private student hostels in Delhi. The submission was made during the hearing of a matter concerning the building collapse in Satya Niketan. A boys' paying-guest accommodation near Delhi University's South Campus had collapsed.

Article Title: Watch: PM Modi grooves at a 'bhajan clubbing' event in Delhi
Article Text:
The Prime Minister has supported the concept in various statements over the year

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi attended on Friday attended a 'Bhajan Clubbing' at Deen Dayal Upadhyay Park in Delhi, on the occasion of Bharatiya Jana Sangh leader Pandit Deendayal Upadhyaya's 110th birth anniversary.The Prime Minister can be seen listening to the Bhajans while playing the headless tambourine or clapping along. The PM also waved to the gathered audience as he arrived for the event.PM Modi has praised Bhajan Clubbing in the past. In January this year, he had praised the youth for embracing the emerging trend of “bhajan-clubbing”, saying it is a powerful blend of devotion, culture, spirituality and modernity that resonates strongly with Gen Z.‘Bhajan-clubbing’ — in which large groups, particularly youngsters, come together in community settings to sing bhajans and devotional songs — Modi said is “no less than global concerts”. He called it a wonderful effort to blend spirituality with modernity while preserving the sanctity of ‘bhajans’, in his monthly broadcast ‘Mann ki Baat’ that month.Then in July, PM Modi had once again praised the concept of "Bhajan Clubbing" during his visit to Australia, saying the trend reflected how young Indians were finding new ways to connect with faith and spirituality. "You must have heard about the new trend of 'Bhajan Clubbing' in India; it is being driven by our Gen Z. Here in Australia, too, I hear that your weekends are filled with faith and spirituality. Whether it is the Lord Satyanarayan Katha at someone's home, Ardas at the Gurudwara, children performing Bhangra or Bharatanatyam, or a cricket tournament in progress--there is always something happening," he had said at the time.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi attended a 'Bhajan Clubbing' at Deen Dayal Upadhyay Park in Delhi. The event was on the occasion of Bharatiya Jana Sangh leader Pandit Deendayal UPadhyaya's 110th birth anniversary. The Prime Minister has supported the concept in various statements over the year.

Not just about surviving crash

Your guide to safer cars

The proposed framework also asks a different question: what happens once the collision has taken place?

What does Bharat NCAP mean for car buyers?

Several countries have their own NCAPS

The bottom line
