Bharat NCAP 2.0, planned for October 2027, will look beyond what happens when a car crashes. The proposed system will examine the entire safety chain: from how a vehicle helps avoid a collision to how well it protects occupants, pedestrians and other vulnerable road users, and what happens after an accident.Union road transport and highways minister Nitin Gadkari announced the proposed timeline at the SIAM Annual Convention in September. The second phase is being planned as the first phase of Bharat New Car Assessment Programme, or Bharat NCAP, approaches the end of its current cycle.According to the ministry of road transport and highways’ draft AIS-197 Revision 1, the first phase of Bharat NCAP began on October 1, 2023 and is valid until September 30, 2027. The draft revision has been prepared as the framework for Bharat NCAP 2.0.The proposed changes could make the safety rating a much broader measure of a car’s performance, not just in a crash, but before, during and after one.Bharat NCAP is India’s own vehicle crash-testing and safety-rating programme. It was formally launched by the ministry of road transport and highways in August 2023 and became operational from October 1, 2023.The programme applies to type-approved passenger vehicles in the M1 category with a gross vehicle weight of less than 3.5 tonnes. It is voluntary, which means manufacturers can offer eligible vehicles for assessment.The programme is anchored by the Central Institute of Road Transport (CIRT), while testing is carried out through designated agencies with the required infrastructure.At its core, Bharat NCAP gives car buyers a common safety benchmark. A vehicle must already meet mandatory regulatory requirements to be sold in India. Bharat NCAP goes a step further by putting eligible vehicles through specified tests and awarding them a rating of between one and five stars.The idea is fairly simple: instead of looking only at a car’s price, design or features, buyers get an additional reference point to understand how the vehicle performs in standardised safety tests.The government has also positioned the programme as a way to encourage manufacturers to improve vehicle safety and strengthen the safety standards of cars made in India.The existing programme broadly assesses three areas:Vehicles are subjected to prescribed crash tests and other assessments. Their performance across these parameters is then used to arrive at the overall star rating.The current framework includes a 64 kmph offset frontal impact test, a 50 kmph side movable deformable barrier test and a pole side impact test, among other checks prescribed under AIS-197.The assessment therefore goes beyond simply asking whether the passenger compartment remains intact.Adult Occupant Protection examines the risk of injury to adults in different crash conditions and seating positions. Child Occupant Protection looks at the protection offered to younger passengers, including the use and installation of child restraint systems.Safety Assist Technologies, meanwhile, covers technologies designed to help prevent crashes or reduce their severity.A car may offer different levels of protection to adults and children, so Bharat NCAP evaluates the two separately.The adult assessment focuses on occupant protection during prescribed crash scenarios, while the child assessment considers how effectively younger occupants are protected and how child restraint systems work within the vehicle.This also means that a car’s overall star rating is not simply a score from one crash test. It reflects performance across several safety parameters.For consumers, the individual scores can therefore provide more information than looking at the star rating alone.Bharat NCAP is anchored by CIRT, with testing carried out through designated testing agencies that have the required facilities.The wider automotive testing ecosystem includes agencies such as the Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI) and the International Centre for Automotive Technology (ICAT).Manufacturers submit eligible vehicles for assessment under the programme. The existing framework specifies procedures around the variant selected for testing, including provisions concerning the base variant of a model.That distinction matters when reading a Bharat NCAP result. A rating should not automatically be assumed to apply to every variant of a model unless the official assessment covers those variants.Bharat NCAP ratings range from one to five stars. A higher rating indicates stronger performance under the programme’s prescribed assessment criteria.But a five-star rating is not a guarantee that occupants will escape injury in every real-world crash. NCAP testing is conducted under standardised conditions and is intended to provide a basis for comparing vehicle safety performance.It is also important to distinguish Bharat NCAP from the mandatory certification requirements for selling a vehicle in India.Bharat NCAP is voluntary and is designed to provide consumers with additional information beyond the mandatory regulatory framework. A vehicle being tested or rated under Bharat NCAP should therefore not be confused with regulatory approval.Since its launch, Bharat NCAP has increasingly become part of the safety conversation around new car launches. The ratings have also become a factor in how manufacturers present their vehicles to consumers, particularly as safety becomes a more visible consideration in the passenger-vehicle market.This is where the proposed second phase takes a much wider approach.The draft AIS-197 Revision 1 divides Bharat NCAP 2.0 into five safety verticals:The change is significant because the current system focuses mainly on occupant protection and safety-assist technologies, while the proposed framework looks at the complete safety chain.The draft framework uses a 100-point assessment structure, with Crash Protection accounting for 55% of the assessment. The remaining weightage covers the other safety areas.In other words, the crash itself will still be a major part of the rating, but it will no longer be the only part of the safety story.Bharat NCAP 2.0 proposes expanding the Crash Protection assessment to five mandatory crash tests:Adult and child occupant protection will continue to be assessed separately.The addition of full-width frontal and rear-impact tests means the proposed system will examine crash scenarios beyond the core tests in the existing framework.That gives the second phase a wider testing footprint and allows different types of impacts to form part of the overall safety assessment.One of the biggest differences in Bharat NCAP 2.0 is that the programme is designed to look at what happens before a crash as well.Crash Avoidance is one of the five proposed verticals. It focuses on technologies and vehicle characteristics that can help prevent a collision or reduce its severity.Safe Driving is another proposed category, widening the assessment beyond the vehicle’s passive protection features.Together, these categories shift the focus from simply asking, “How well does this car perform when it crashes?” to a broader question: “How does this vehicle contribute to safety across different stages of a road incident?”Bharat NCAP 2.0 also proposes a separate Vulnerable Road User Protection category. This brings pedestrians and other vulnerable road users more directly into the safety assessment.Post-Crash Safety is one of the five proposed assessment areas. Minister Gadkari described Bharat NCAP 2.0 as covering the entire safety chain, including post-crash evacuation and care. “We are going to evaluate the entire crash chain,” Gadkari said, adding that new technologies developed globally as well as by startups would be considered under the programme.This means the assessment is intended to extend beyond the instant of impact and examine safety considerations in the period immediately after a crash.It adds another layer to the programme’s approach: avoiding the crash where possible, protecting people during the impact, and addressing safety after the collision.For buyers, Bharat NCAP offers an additional way to compare cars beyond mandatory safety requirements.A consumer can look at a vehicle’s overall rating as well as its adult and child protection performance and the safety technologies considered in the assessment.The rating is not meant to replace other factors involved in buying a car. Price, size, fuel efficiency, features, driving requirements and other considerations remain relevant, but the proposed 2.0 framework would expand that information further.Buyers could eventually have a broader picture of how a car performs across crash protection, crash avoidance, safe driving, vulnerable-road-user protection and post-crash safety.Bharat NCAP is one part of a much larger road-safety challenge, focusing on the structure of vehicles. Vehicle design and safety technology can influence the outcome of a crash, but they cannot address every reason why accidents happen.The ministry has identified several factors associated with road crashes, including speeding, mobile-phone use, drunken driving, wrong-side driving, lane indiscipline, jumping red lights and failure to use helmets and seat belts. Vehicle condition, road conditions and weather can also play a role.Government data recorded 1,68,491 road accident fatalities in 2022.Bharat NCAP therefore addresses one part of this wider equation: the safety performance of vehicles. Its proposed second phase would broaden that role by looking at what a vehicle can do to help avoid crashes, how it protects people when a crash occurs, how it protects vulnerable road users and what happens afterwards.The current Bharat NCAP phase remains valid until September 30, 2027. The government has proposed introducing Bharat NCAP 2.0 from October 2027, with the draft AIS-197 Revision 1 serving as the framework for the next phase.The proposed transition would take India’s vehicle safety-rating system from a relatively focused crash and occupant-protection programme to a broader safety assessment.The familiar one-to-five-star rating would remain the consumer-facing language of vehicle safety, but the assessment behind it is set to become much more comprehensive.The bigger shift is in the question Bharat NCAP is trying to answer. Instead of looking only at how a car performs when it is involved in a crash, the proposed system would examine the vehicle’s safety journey from avoiding a collision to protecting occupants and vulnerable road users, and supporting safety after the crash.That could give Indian car buyers a wider set of safety information to consider when choosing their next vehicle.
Article Summary: Bharat NCAP is India’s own vehicle crash-testing and safety-rating programme. It was formally launched by the ministry of road transport and highways in August 2023 and became operational from October 1, 2023. The current framework includes a 64 kmph frontal impact test, a 50 kmph side side test and other checks. The proposed changes could make the safety rating a much broader measure of a car's performance.

Article Title: Intel cuts VP ranks from 450 to 200, CFO David Zinsner calls it a 'cultural problem'; says it contributed to products going through four or five...
Article Text:
Intel's leadership was hearing a different story from the one on the ground

Intel says 18A yields and 14A progress show the overhaul is working

Intel has cut the number of vice presidents at the company from about 450 at its peak to roughly 200. It has also halved its management layers from 12 to six as CEO Lip-Bu Tan tries to get the chipmaker to decide faster and ship on time. CFO David Zinsner shared the numbers at the Deutsche Bank Technology Conference, describing the old structure as a cultural problem that hurt Intel's execution for more than a decade.Zinsner said too many people across the organisation held veto power, so decisions kept stalling. The damage showed up in products. Chips often needed four or five development cycles before they were ready, when they should have reached production after the first attempt. Looking back at the last decade, he said much of Intel's trouble "can be boiled down to culture," adding that 50-person startups were getting products out faster than Intel.Transparency was the other big issue. According to Zinsner, information changed as it moved up the management chain, and by the time presentations reached the CEO, they often described a different situation from the one teams lower down knew about.He did not frame this as deliberate deception. Some managers simply did not want to admit a project was failing. The result was that Intel's top leadership sometimes made decisions based on an inaccurate picture of the business. Tan has since brought in executives he trusts who are used to working in leaner organisations.The VP cuts sit inside a much larger downsizing. Intel had 108,900 employees at the end of 2024 and 88,400 by late September 2025, including subsidiaries like Mobileye. Around 20,500 of those exits happened under Tan, who took charge in March 2025 and told staff there would be "no more blank checks." The pitch was about flattening management, but in Oregon only 8% of the laid-off employees had "manager" in their job titles. Most were engineers and technicians.Zinsner pointed to early signs of change. Several products have reached A-stepping, Intel's term for the first version of a chip, without the repeated development cycles that were once routine. Intel 18A yields are running ahead of internal milestones, and 14A defect density is tracking better than the company's target curve.Intel is now preparing for 14A risk production in 2027 and high-volume manufacturing in 2028. Internal product teams have started designing for the process, and interest from external foundry customers has picked up.Finances are moving too. Intel entered 2026 expecting gross margins in the high 30s and is now in the low 40s. The target is the mid-40s, then the high 40s, and eventually a figure starting with 5. To get there, Intel uses an internal "Rule of 45" that combines revenue growth and operating margin. Slower businesses must deliver stronger margins, while faster-growing ones can earn more investment.Halving the VP ranks gives Intel a leaner org chart, but the numbers Zinsner shared will only mean something if they hold. 14A is the first major process being developed entirely under Tan's structure, with fewer layers between engineers and the CEO and fewer people who can block a decision. If it reaches risk production in 2027 and volume manufacturing in 2028 as planned, it will be the clearest evidence yet that the cultural reset worked. If it slips into the multiple development cycles that marked the last decade, the 250 fewer vice presidents will have changed very little.
Article Summary: Intel has cut the number of vice presidents at the company from about 450 at its peak to roughly 200. It has also halved its management layers from 12 to six as CEO Lip-Bu Tan tries to get the chipmaker to decide faster and ship on time.Intel says 18A yields and 14A progress show the overhaul is working.

Article Title: Microsoft shakes up communications team; CEO Satya Nadella and President Brad Smith sends memo to employees, says 'We will likely have more employees and executives acting as ...'
Article Text:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella described the communications shake-up as a response to a media environment

Why is Microsoft changing its communications strategy

Microsoft communications team will now report to Brad Smith

What happens to Microsoft communications chief Frank Shaw

Microsoft is changing how it communicates with the outside world. The company is moving its communications team out of its marketing organisation and into the corporate, external and legal affairs group led by Vice Chair and President Brad Smith, according to internal memos from Smith and CEO Satya Nadella . The bigger change, however, may be how Microsoft employees speak for the company. Nadella said the company wants engineers, sellers, partners and other employees who are close to its products and customers to play a bigger role in telling Microsoft's story.“We will likely have more employees and executives acting as part of Microsoft’s public voice, including on social media,” Smith wrote in his memo.Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella described the communications shake-up as a response to a media environment that has become “increasingly fragmented and noisier than ever.” Instead of relying mainly on a central communications team to shape Microsoft's public messaging, the CEO wants people closer to the company's work to have a greater role.“In many ways, the people closest to the work have the best opportunity to shape how Microsoft is understood,” Nadella wrote. He said Microsoft wants engineers, sellers, partners and others “closest to our products and customers” to become “an even bigger part of how we tell our story, all connected by a shared strategy and set of principles.”Nadella added: “We will learn, we will experiment, and we will evolve. There is a fundamentally new way to think about communications, and this team will be central to building it.”Under the new structure, Microsoft's communications function will sit within the organisation led by President Brad Smith rather than under marketing. Smith's organisation handles Microsoft's legal, regulatory and public policy work, including antitrust matters, litigation and government relations.The communications team will therefore sit alongside these functions, although Microsoft plans to continue coordination between communications and marketing.Satya Nadella described Smith as one of the few Microsoft leaders who “embody Microsoft’s voice” authentically. He also praised Smith's “rare ability to communicate complex ideas with clarity, conviction, and trust.”The restructuring also changes the role of longtime Microsoft communications chief Frank X. Shaw. Shaw announced earlier this month that he would leave Microsoft at the end of the year after more than two decades with the company. He will now step away from his current responsibilities and serve as an adviser to Smith and interim communications leader Brent Colburn during the transition.Microsoft said Shaw will remain with the company through the end of the year. Shaw described the latest development as the formalisation of the plan that had already been announced.Microsoft said Shaw “has been a trusted counselor and leader at Microsoft for more than two decades, and we’re grateful he will continue to act as an advisor during the transition.”Satya Nadella also thanked Shaw for his contribution. He said Shaw has “made tremendous contributions to the company and to our communications function over the last 17+ years” and has been “a great source of counsel to our leadership team and to me personally, across the company’s biggest moments.”Smith also praised Shaw, saying he had “worked as closely with him as almost anyone” over the years. Smith added that Shaw's “enduring impact on Microsoft and this team will be felt for years to come. I will miss him.”
Article Summary: Microsoft is moving its communications team out of its marketing organisation and into the corporate, external and legal affairs group led by Vice Chair and President Brad Smith. The bigger change, however, may be how Microsoft employees speak for the company. Nadella said the company wants engineers, sellers, partners and other employees who are close to its products and customers to play a bigger role.

Article Title: Budget phones are disappearing fast, report says by 2030, 40% of sub-Rs 20,000 smartphones may be gone
Article Text:
Why budget phones’ shipment will squeeze

Smartphone shipment rebound expected through 2030

The era of the budget smartphones is rapidly shrinking. Over 230 million annual smartphone shipments priced below $200 (Rs 20,000) will vanish from worldwide retail channels between 2025 and 2030, a report has said. According to Counterpoint Research’s Smartphone Shipment Forecast by Price Band tracker, this segment will contract by roughly 40% through the end of the decade. The decline comes even as total worldwide smartphone shipments stage a broader rebound back toward 2025 volumes.The disappearing budget tier stems largely from structural aftershocks linked to the 2026–2027 industry downturn. A combination of rising prices for mobile chipsets and memory, higher baseline hardware requirements and phone makers scaling back unprofitable market footprints has made entry-level devices increasingly hard to sustain, the report said, adding, as components eat up a far larger share of total build costs on inexpensive devices, manufacturers have virtually no room to absorb price jumps.It also said that rather than buying brand-new budget handsets, consumers are responding in several ways. For example, users are delaying upgrades and extending how long they keep their existing devices. Some buyers are turning to certified refurbished and second-hand phones, and a portion of buyers is moving up into higher price tiers via installment plans.“The smartphone market will recover in unit terms, but the affordable segment will not return to its previous standing.The opportunity now shifts toward better-specced mainstream devices and premium products, although higher tiers cannot absorb all the lost volume. The result will be a market that is similar in overall size but materially different in value and competitive profile. There is also a wider connectivity risk, as the loss of affordable new smartphones could make it harder for first-time users in lower-income markets to come online,” said Yang Wang, Principal Analyst at Counterpoint Research.Counterpoint estimates that overall smartphone deliveries will climb back to approximately 1.20 billion units by 2030, just behind 2025 benchmark levels. The stagnation across the mid-range highlights that budget volume is not simply flowing upward in a straight line. Instead, delayed purchase cycles and disappearing first-time buyer demand mean higher tiers will not make up for all the lost volume under $200.Across developing and lower-income markets, device affordability remains the single greatest roadblock to mobile internet access. As sub-$200 options disappear, the transition from basic feature phones or shared family devices to personal smartphone ownership risks slowing to a crawl. This slowdown threatens to complicate long-term efforts by network operators, software developers, and governments seeking to broaden digital public infrastructure, localized content and mobile financial services.
Article Summary: Over 230 million annual smartphone shipments priced below $200 (Rs 20,000) will vanish from worldwide retail channels between 2025 and 2030. The disappearing budget tier stems largely from structural aftershocks linked to the 2026–2027 industry downturn. Counterpoint estimates that overall smartphone deliveries will climb back to approximately 1.20 billion units by 2030.

Article Title: Google, OpenAI and Anthropic may launch AI safety standard by early 2027
Article Text:
Momentum builds following safety proposals

Google, OpenAI and Anthropic are said to be collaborating to establish an independent artificial intelligence (AI) safety body by late 2026 or early 2027, a report from The Information has claimed, adding that they have reached out to former White House AI policy advisor Sriram Krishnan to serve as chief executive. The report says that the planned organisation, provisionally named the Standards Authority for Frontier AI (SAFA), will operate independently of government administration. Its primary mission will be to define practical benchmarks for the three companies' public safety pledges and provide direct support to developers evaluating cutting-edge models prior to commercial deployment.Citing people familiar with the initiative, the report said that apart from Krishnan, the companies have reached out to Arati Prabhakar, former director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, to take the top post at SAFA. The three technology giants are also weighing whether SAFA should conduct direct model assessments in-house.While the United States Center for AI Standards and Innovation already handles federal evaluation, insiders noted persistent concerns that the government agency lacks adequate technical and financial resources to thoroughly inspect complex frontier systems.The push toward a joint authority follows weeks of escalating industry dialogue.About 10 days ago, an OpenAI spokesperson confirmed to CNBC that the company was holding active talks with Google and Anthropic regarding coordinated safety frameworks. These discussions gained momentum following a proposal published on X in July by Sir Demis Hassabis, co-founder of Google DeepMind and Alphabet’s chief scientist. Hassabis argued for a US-backed standards body modeled after a public-private partnership or a self-regulatory watchdog, drawing comparisons to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).While Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI remain locked in a race for commercial dominance, leadership across all three firms has faced mounting scrutiny over potential catastrophic and security risks. The momentum toward collective oversight accelerated earlier this month after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei released an essay calling for an industrywide slowdown in the release of frontier models to allow safety mechanisms to catch up.
Article Summary: Google, OpenAI and Anthropic are said to be collaborating to establish an independent artificial intelligence (AI) safety body by late 2026 or early 2027. The planned organisation, provisionally named the Standards Authority for Frontier AI (SAFA), will operate independently of government administration. Its primary mission will be to define practical benchmarks for the three companies' public safety pledges.

Article Title: Amazon Prime refund eligibility expanded to more customers; company to start giving up to $200 from October 1; new changes remove need to file claims
Article Text:
Amazon Prime refund eligibility expanded to more customers; company to start giving up to $200 from October 1; new changes remove need to file claims

What was the lawsuit about

allegedly enrolled tens of millions of customers in Amazon Prime subscriptions without their knowledge or consent

made it difficult for customers to cancel their Amazon Prime subscriptions.

Who is eligible for a refund

You are an Amazon Prime customer in the United States.

You signed up for an Amazon Prime subscription through a “challenged enrollment flow” or tried to cancel through the online cancellation flow but were unable to do so between June 23, 2019 and June 23, 2025.

through a “challenged enrollment flow” or tried to cancel through the online cancellation flow but were unable to do so between June 23, 2019 and June 23, 2025. You used no more than 20 Amazon Prime Benefits (including Prime Music or Prime Video products offered for free to Prime subscribers) in any 12-month period following Amazon Prime enrollment.

How do I get my payment

When will I get my payment

How much will my payment be

I didn’t get a refund, now what

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has expanded the eligibility of Amazon Prime customers who will get refunds of up to $200. Following the landmark $2.5 billion settlement reached by the Trump-Vance FTC, Amazon started sending payments in November 2025 to eligible Prime customers affected by misleading enrollment and cancellation practices. By September 2026, Amazon issued over $845 million in refunds to eligible Prime customers. FTC has now revised the settlement with Amazon, making more Prime customers eligible for the refund. Under the revised settlement order, Amazon will send automatic refunds to eligible Prime customers starting October 1.According to the FTC’s lawsuit, Amazon:As the result of the Trump-Vance FTC’s historic settlement, Amazon is required to pay $1.5 billion for refunds to customers affected by its unlawful Prime enrollment and cancellation practices. Amazon is also required to pay a $1 billion civil penalty and cease unlawful enrollment and cancellation practices for Prime subscriptions.Under the revised settlement order, you are eligible for a refund if you meet all three requirements:The “challenged enrollment flows” are universal Prime decision page, shipping selection page, single page checkout, or the Prime Video enrollment flow.No action is needed to receive a refund. You do not have to file a claim, respond to a notice, or complete any forms.Amazon will send automatic payments to eligible customers.If you are eligible, no action is needed. Amazon will send automatic refund payments by mailed check or electronic payment (PayPal or Venmo). Payments expire 60 days after the issue date. Please accept your payment on time.If you need help with your payment, please contact Amazon at admin@SubscriptionMembershipSettlement.com.If you are eligible, you will get your refund by April 2027.Eligible Prime customers will receive refunds for their Amazon Prime subscription fees, with a maximum total payment of $200. Earlier payments under the order were capped at $51 per eligible customer. Under the revised settlement order, Amazon may issue additional payments of up to $149 per eligible customer, bringing the maximum total payment to $200.Only eligible Prime customers will get a refund.
Article Summary: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has expanded the eligibility of Amazon Prime customers who will get refunds of up to $200. Under the revised settlement order, Amazon will send automatic refunds to eligible Prime customers starting October 1. Amazon is required to pay $1.5 billion for refunds to customers affected by its unlawful enrollment and cancellation practices.

Article Title: In 2018, a Nebraska caregiver lost his home over a $588 tax debt; after a six-year court fight, he got the title back
Article Text:
AI generated representative image of property at sale. (Image Credit: Chatgpt)

The Supreme Court gets involved

Image of the United States Supreme Court (Image Credit: Wikimedia)

A bittersweet ending

A Scottsbluff homeowner has successfully recovered the legal title to his residential property after losing it over a $588 property tax delinquency, AP News reported. The case ultimately reached the Supreme Court which established that a homeowner’s surplus equity is protected from confiscation under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution. Fair and his late wife, Terry, had lived in the home for nearly two decades and had already paid off its mortgage by the early 2010s.The legal dispute traces back to 2013, when Kevin Fair's wife was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. Looking to provide full-time care at home, Fair resigned from his occupation, which led the household to default on their 2014 property tax bill of $588, the outlet reported. Pursuant to the Nebraska code active during that time, Scotts Bluff County issued a tax lien to a private investment firm by the name Continental Resources.Over three years, the firm paid the ongoing taxes while the debt accrued at an interest rate of 14 percent. Once the accumulated fees, penalties and interest totaled $5,268 in 2018, it prompted the county to hand over the home's full title and $60,000 in equity to the investor, rendering the Fairs with no compensation. At the time, Pacific Legal Foundation noted that at least a dozen states, including Nebraska, permitted counties the right to seize homes over unpaid taxes without returning any remaining equity to homeowners.Fair’s initial civil lawsuit contended that while the municipality's right to recover tax debts remains paramount, it's unconstitutional to confiscate a property's entire equity beyond the actual debt threshold. The Nebraska Supreme Court initially declined this claim in March 2022, after a year, the U.S. Supreme Court cited its landmark ruling in Tyler v. Hennepin County, a Minnesota case, and ordered the state court to reconsider.After that, a unanimous Supreme Court ruled that the government cannot seize more than what is strictly owed in public debts, holding that any remaining equity belongs explicitly to the homeowner. Aided by the new U.S. Supreme Court precedent, Fair's legal team (Pacific Legal Foundation) pulled off the gambit to have the initial ruling overturned. By August 2024, the Nebraska Supreme Court officially took sides with Fair, with the declaration that he was owed just compensation for the seizure. Following the ruling, Christina Martin, senior attorney at Pacific Legal Foundation, said the decision confirmed that home equity is protected by the Constitution, and the outcome saved Fair from homelessness, according to AP News.The eventual retrieval of Fair’s property came with a personal cost as he lost his wife to health complications in 2019 leaving him to attend the litigation process alone. Furthermore, Fair suffered a major stroke shortly before the final title transfer was completed. Stepping up, community members organized a public crowdfunding campaign, which raised $16,000 to fix any upcoming tax obligations, general home repairs, and wheelchair ramp construction for the ailing widower. Contemplating his early skepticism, Fair had previously conveyed to his legal team he was quite dubious whether the national court would have the time or interest to hear the case of an average person from Western Nebraska.Though Fair managed to retain his home during his final days, he passed away on January 17, 2025, as per Pacific Legal Foundation leaving behind a permanent statutory footprint. While the Nebraska Legislature had passed LB 727 in 2023, abolishing home equity theft statewide, Fair's personal victory required a multi-year courtroom battle to reclaim his title, according to Pacific Legal Foundation. Today, PLF says it is using the precedent to challenge similar foreclosure practices.
Article Summary: Kevin Fair and his late wife, Terry, had lived in the home for nearly two decades and had already paid off its mortgage by the early 2010s. Scotts Bluff County issued a tax lien to a private investment firm by the name Continental Resources over three years. Once the accumulated fees, penalties and interest totaled $5,268 in 2018, it prompted the county to hand over the home's full title and $60,000 in equity to the investor, rendering the Fairs with no compensation.

Article Title: India’s travel map is changing: Shorter trips, more pilgrimages, UP on top
Article Text:
From the Taj Mahal to Kerala’s backwaters and Varanasi’s ghats, India’s travel map is being redefined

Move over Kerala and Goa: Uttar Pradesh is now India's top travel pick

UP is leading tourism

It's not a holiday, it's a pilgrimage: Faith still drives half of India's travel

Faith still drives India's tourism

The vanishing two-week vacation: Why Indians are travelling more but staying less

Weddings, hospitals, shrines: The real reasons Indians are packing their bags

Bus or train? How rural and urban India travel differently

The travel divide

Why Kerala's tourists are mostly... Keralites: India's hyperlocal travel boom





NEW DELHI: For a country that has never really stopped moving, India's roads, railway platforms and highway dhabas have suddenly turned even busier. But look closely, and the crowd isn't quite what you'd expect.It isn't the family piling into a car for a fortnight at the hills. It's a two-day dash to a shrine, a hurried visit to a sick relative, a wedding two states away, a quick escape squeezed between weekends. India's holiday, it turns out, is shrinking — even as the country travels more than ever before.The numbers capture the scale of that movement. The Ministry of Tourism's latest dashboard recorded 4,286.9 million domestic tourist visits, or 428.69 crore, in 2025 — 45.6% more than the previous year, and nearly 85% above the 2019 pre-pandemic level.But the bigger story lies beyond the record number. A new Domestic Tourism Expenditure Survey by the National Statistical Office, conducted between July 2025 and June 2026 across 2.46 lakh households, offers a closer look at where Indians are going, why they are travelling, and what their journeys actually look like.Uttar Pradesh has emerged as the biggest destination in the latest survey, accounting for 15.7% of domestic overnight visitor-trips over the preceding 365 days.Tamil Nadu followed with 13.4%, while Rajasthan accounted for 8%.The pattern holds even when the window is narrowed to the previous 30 days for business, social, education and other purposes.UP accounted for 15.5% of visitor-trips, followed by Bihar at 10.5% and Tamil Nadu at 9.6%, according to the NSO survey.The UP story also extends well beyond its most familiar postcards. The Uttar Pradesh Department data shows Chitrakoot's visits rising from 1.18 crore in 2024 to 3.65 crore in 2025, while Mirzapur climbed from 1.41 crore to 2.10 crore.The state is also developing experiential and rural tourism across 230 villages.For all the talk of leisure, India's domestic travel story remains deeply rooted in faith. The NSO survey found that pilgrimage and religious activity accounted for 48% of overnight trips in the 365-day category, the largest share for both rural and urban households.That doesn't mean India's tourism boom is simply a pilgrimage boom. Rather, it shows how religious travel has become one of the country's biggest engines of domestic movement, often pulling visitors towards destinations that combine faith with history, culture, food and local commerce.The government's own tourism data reflects the scale of the change at major pilgrimage centres. According to information provided by the Uttar Pradesh government to the Ministry of Tourism, Ayodhya recorded 16.44 crore visitors in 2024, compared with about 60.23 lakh in 2020.The Ministry has also sanctioned projects under PRASHAD and other tourism schemes aimed at improving infrastructure at pilgrimage and heritage destinations.The religious map is not limited to one faith circuit or one state. Government tourism programmes include projects around Buddhist, Ramayana, heritage and pilgrimage destinations across several parts of the country.The implication is visible in the data: faith remains a major reason to travel, but many of these journeys spill over into a broader tourism experience.The latest survey suggests that the classic idea of a long annual vacation may account for only part of India's travel economy.An average overnight trip involved 2.03 visitors, while around 80% of visitors stayed for five days or less. In the separate category of overnight trips undertaken in the previous 30 days, around 45% lasted only two to three days.That means the tourism boom is being fuelled not merely by more people taking holidays, but by people travelling more frequently, and for much shorter stretches.The reasons Indians travel are just as varied as the destinations.Pilgrimage and religious travel accounted for 48% of overnight trips in the 365-day category. But the survey also shows a sharp rural-urban divide: health and medical travel made up 38.4% of rural overnight trips, while holidaying, leisure and recreation accounted for 36.4% of urban overnight trips.The 30-day data brings another dimension into view: 89% of overnight visitor-trips in that category were for social purposes.Weddings, family visits and other social obligations form a major part of the country's travel economy, even though they may never appear in the conventional image of tourism.The way Indians travel changes sharply with where they live.For overnight trips related to leisure, pilgrimage, health and shopping over the past year, buses accounted for 32% of visitor-trips among rural households, while trains had the highest share among urban households at 35%.Over that same year-long period, hotels and guesthouses accounted for 36% of urban overnight visitor-trips, while non-commercial accommodation had the biggest share in rural India at 28%.For the shorter 30-day category, buses remained dominant across the board, accounting for 48% of rural and 44% of urban visitor-trips.Kerala offers a telling example. The state recorded 2.51 crore domestic tourist visits in 2025, up 12.64% from 2024. Yet 68.33% of its domestic visitors were from within Kerala, followed by Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, according to Kerala Tourism data.That suggests India's tourism map isn't simply about people crossing state borders to reach famous destinations. A substantial part of the movement is happening much closer to home.And that may be the most revealing change of all: India's tourism boom is no longer just about where Indians go on holiday. It is increasingly about how often they move, what takes them there, how long they stay, and how far they really need to travel to call it a trip.
Article Summary: Uttar Pradesh has emerged as the biggest destination in the latest survey, accounting for 15.7% of domestic overnight visitor-trips over the preceding 365 days. The pattern holds even when the window is narrowed to the previous 30 days for business, social, education and other purposes.

Article Title: At 8, Meera Mehta sold chocolates to raise Rs 1 lakh for animal welfare; by 21, Mumbai medical student's decade-long fundraising had crossed Rs 1.5 crore
Article Text:
Meera Mehta (21) has raised over Rs 1.5 crore.

From selling chocolates to raising Rs 1.5 crore

Then Covid-19 changed the scale of her work

A decade of fundraising, one campaign at a time





MUMBAI: At six, Meera Mehta began volunteering. Two years later, she and a group of children tried something simple to raise money for a cause they cared about — they sold chocolates. The effort brought in Rs 1 lakh, which was used to rehabilitate animals. By the time Mehta was 21, that childhood initiative had grown into a decade-long fundraising journey, with more than Rs 1.5 crore raised for projects related to healthcare and education.A third-year MBBS student at MGM College in Navi Mumbai, Mehta received the Diana Award in 2020 for her fundraising and volunteering work. The award recognised young people aged between nine and 25 for social action and humanitarian work. Her volunteering was closely linked to South Gujarat. Mehta was a volunteer with Shrimad Rajchandra Love and Care, where her work included supporting projects in healthcare, education and community development.Her fundraising over the previous 10 years had supported the Dharampur hospital in Valsad district, Shrimad Rajchandra Vidyapeeth — a science college for tribal youth — tree-plantation drives and skill-development programmes for women in villages in South Gujarat.The scale of the fundraising was striking considering how it had started. Mehta told TOI that when she was eight, she and others sold chocolates and raised Rs 1 lakh to help rehabilitate animals. She subsequently began raising funds regularly through the Mumbai Marathon and other efforts.Her work took on a different urgency in 2020, when the Covid-19 pandemic left vulnerable communities struggling for food, transport and basic protective equipment. During the pandemic, Mehta raised more than Rs 33 lakh, TOI reported. The money was used for several forms of assistance, including sponsoring two buses for migrant workers travelling to Bihar, providing meals to daily wagers and distributing PPE kits and masks to frontline workers. By July 2020, she was still raising money and had set herself a target of reaching Rs 50 lakh through her pandemic fundraising campaign. The fundraising came while Mehta was continuing her medical studies in Navi Mumbai. "While I continue to raise funds, I am also studying hard to become a doctor and serve tribal children better," Mehta told TOI.Her efforts had also brought recognition before the Diana Award. In 2019, Mehta was selected as an 'Inspirational Change Agent' at the Mumbai Marathon alongside boxer Mary Kom for her fundraising work. But the numbers were only part of her story. What began when she was six with volunteering had led to a chocolate-selling fundraiser at eight. That first campaign raised Rs 1 lakh. Over the next decade, the fundraising grew to more than Rs 1.5 crore, supporting healthcare, education, animal rehabilitation and community projects. And when the pandemic created a new set of needs in 2020, Mehta continued fundraising — this time raising more than Rs 33 lakh to help migrant workers, daily wagers and frontline workers.
Article Summary: Meera Mehta, 21, has raised more than Rs 1.5 crore for projects related to healthcare and education. She received the Diana Award in 2020 for her fundraising and volunteering work. Her work took on a different urgency in 2020 when the Covid-19 pandemic left vulnerable communities struggling for food, transport and basic protective equipment.

Article Title: Tax auction blunder resolved: Couple sells mistakenly acquired land for $26,000; reflects on bureaucratic ordeal and lessons learned
Article Text:
Representative image of a neighbourhood in San Francisco. Image Credit: Chatgpt

Misleading caused celebration and devastation at the same time

Respresentative image of A quiet alley lined with wooden fences. Image Credit: Pexels.

An artist concludes the real estate debacle

In San Francisco, a couple accidentally bought a side street at a tax auction for $25,000 and later resold it for $26,000, CBS News reported. Homeowners JJ Hollingsworth and Alemayehu Mergia spent remorseful months after a sealed bid they won mistakenly gave them keys to a 83-foot-by-7-foot strip of land rather than the neighboring $1 million duplex. The recent private transaction concludes their exhausting bureaucratic ordeal with the city's tax collector's office.The couple was initially misled by a sealed-bid auction notice from the San Francisco Treasurer and Tax Collector for the property at 1926 Kirkham St. Believing they were bidding on a two-unit rental building, they submitted a $25,000 cashier's check and an $8,000 transfer tax check, calculated based on the home's roughly $1 million value, as they say they were advised to do by the city. Hollingsworth said they would have always regretted not seizing the moment, wondering what could have happened otherwise.Believing themselves to be the new owners, the couple celebrated with family and friends and even dropped by the Kirkham Street duplex to introduce themselves to the tenants. However, the reality of the mix-up seeped in when the city returned all of their $8,000 transfer tax.This brought about the realization that instead of the duplex they owned an unusable fire lane called the "Dirt Alley".Maintaining their position, municipal tax officials through Amanda Kahn Fried, chief of policy and communications claimed that all documents related to public auction were clearly identified and flagged the plots as unusable by their size, location, or other conditions. A sealed auction included 47 plots, out of which half of them were already sold. Four of those plots were offloaded for just $1 apiece, while the rest generated a sum ranging from $10 to $11,000. The couple's $25,000 bid was much higher in comparison to any other winning bid in the auction.San Francisco's Board of Supervisors is notorious for never reversing tax sales, doing so only once, in the 2017 Presidio Terrace case , per Board of Supervisors File No. 171281. The couple remained in legal limbo until the stalemate finally broke when a private buyer approached them with an unexpected inquiry.Things took a turn for the better when Hollingsworth unexpectedly received a written letter from an interested buyer, an artist who explained he wanted to purchase the parcel. While initially dubious of the request, a subsequent meeting was enough to ease all of the qualms Hollingsworth had. When told by the potential buyer that his endeavor is to paint a quilt in the alley, it was enough to get Hollingsworth on board.Before signing off the $26,000 contract, Hollingsworth took the aid of an attorney to thoroughly vet the buyer to look for any checkered history. The deal was finalized with legal provisions added directly to the deed, which ensured the couple and their surrounding neighbors maintain permanent physical access to the lane.The closure of the sale brought immense elation to the household, concluding a period of eager anticipation. Mergia described feeling a strong sense of relief following the closing. Despite a good ending to close off such an ordeal the couple remain highly critical of the city's tax paperwork layout. Hollingsworth said because of the ordeal, she had learned a hard lesson on reading auction paperwork closely, and that she believes the city should learn one too. Even after the mistake was resolved, the property had briefly been listed on Zillow as a sold, one-bedroom, one-bathroom, 850-square-foot residential dwelling, CBS News reported.
Article Summary: Homeowners JJ Hollingsworth and Alemayehu Mergia spent remorseful months after a sealed bid they won mistakenly gave them keys to a 83-foot-by-7-foot strip of land. The couple remained in legal limbo until the stalemate finally broke when a private buyer approached them with an unexpected inquiry.
